White-chinned petrel chicks hatch after an incubation period that is tightly coupled to nest temperature. Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 58.9 days [ab = approximately 58.9 days], a duration that falls within the typical 55 to 65 day range reported for this species. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is remarkably low, with field measurements recording a birth mass of just 92.6 grams [Wwb = 92.6 grams]. This modest initial weight reflects the relatively small yolk reserves available to the embryo and the substantial energetic cost of the prolonged incubation period. The newly emerged chick is entirely dependent on biparental provisioning, and its initial body condition at this stage provides a critical foundation for the rapid somatic growth that must occur in the ensuing weeks before it can achieve thermal independence.

The developmental trajectory of the nestling is characterized by a swift accumulation of mass, driven by frequent meals of fish and cephalopods delivered by both parents. The initial wet weight at hatching is recorded at 120 grams [Ww0 = 120 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the chick upon emergence from the egg. Over the subsequent weeks, the chick undergoes a period of exponential growth, fueled by the high-lipid diet typical of procellariiform seabirds. This phase is energetically demanding, and the rate of mass gain is closely linked to the frequency of foraging trips by the adults, which can be influenced by local prey availability and oceanographic conditions. The rapid transition from a 120 gram [Ww0 = 120 gram] neonate to a far heftier pre-fledging mass represents one of the most physiologically intensive periods in the life cycle of this pelagic predator.

As the breeding season progresses, the developing chick prepares for its first flight, a milestone that marks the culmination of the nestling period. Under the core body temperature typical of an actively metabolizing bird (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), the time from hatching to fledging averages 98.1 days [tx = 98.1 days]. This extended fledging period is characteristic of many large procellariids and allows for the complete development of flight feathers and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to sustain the chick through the critical post-fledging period when it must learn to forage independently. The achievement of sustained flight at this age represents a pivotal transition from a sedentary, provisioning-dependent existence to the mobile, self-sufficient lifestyle required for survival at sea. The fledgling departs the nest with a body mass that is often close to adult proportions.

Sexual maturity in the White-chinned petrel is not attained until well after the fledgling has left the nest and spent several years at sea acquiring foraging experience and body condition. The age at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, has been estimated at 294.3 days after hatching [tp = 294.3 days after hatching], again measured under a metabolic body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively delayed maturation is a common life-history strategy among long-lived seabirds, allowing individuals to invest heavily in somatic growth and learning before committing to the high energetic demands of reproduction. However, actual first breeding typically occurs considerably later than the onset of physiological puberty, as young birds must first compete for nest sites and establish pair bonds within dense colonies. The interval between reaching sexual maturity and successfully raising a first brood can span multiple years, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at 730 days [tR = 730 days].
